screens.title: Database Maintenance & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Maintenance keeps a database healthy and predictable. Over time, updates and deletions leave behind overhead that slows queries and consumes disk space. In PostgreSQL this shows up as dead tuples and table bloat; routine commands reclaim space and refresh the planner's statistics so queries run efficiently. In this lesson you will learn what VACUUM and ANALYZE do, when to prefer lightweight background maintenance versus aggressive operations, and why some maintenance commands must be scheduled carefully to avoid locking production tables. We'll also preview reindexing, integrity checks, and log management so you can spot when a table or index needs attention. Finally, you'll be introduced to a practical activity that walks through creating simulated bloat, running VACUUM ANALYZE, and checking sizes before and after. By the end you will understand not just the commands but the operational trade-offs: which actions are safe to run continuously, which require a maintenance window, and how to measure success. Consider how routine care prevents surprises during critical analysis jobs or nightly batch runs. What maintenance step would you prioritize first on a heavily updated table?

screens.title: Why routine maintenance matters
screens.narratorSegment: Databases need routine care because internal file structures evolve as data changes. When rows are updated or deleted, many systems do not immediately overwrite physical storage; instead they mark earlier versions as obsolete. Over time those obsolete entries accumulate, increasing the amount of data the server must scan for queries and the space required on disk. This leads to slower scans, higher input and output, and sometimes unexpected disk-full conditions during peak workloads. Maintenance tasks like VACUUM and reindexing remove or rebuild these remnants so the system can work with a leaner physical dataset. Beyond space, maintenance also keeps metadata and statistics accurate; stale statistics lead the planner to choose slower execution plans and make even well-indexed queries perform poorly. Neglect can also raise the chance of corruption going unnoticed, which is why integrity checks are part of routine work. A practical misconception is thinking that infrequent heavy maintenance is equivalent to continuous light maintenance. In practice, small automated actions are safer and keep disruption low. Which recurring checks would you include in a weekly maintenance checklist for a workload that writes a lot of small updates?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Why routine maintenance matters
Definition & consequences
  • Dead tuples and fragmentation increase the data volume the server scans.
  • Stale planner statistics cause suboptimal execution plans.
  • Log files and unreclaimed space can exhaust disk if unrotated.
Analogy
Think of a database like a workshop bench. Leaving scraps and tools scattered makes tasks slower and more error prone. Regular cleaning keeps the bench efficient.
Practical signs of neglect
Slow sequential scans
Rapid growth in pg_relation_size
Rising disk I/O wait times
Large, unrotated log files
Key Takeaway

Plan lightweight, frequent maintenance to keep performance predictable and reduce the need for disruptive, locking operations.

screens.title: Dead Tuples and Table Bloat
screens.narratorSegment: A dead tuple is an old row version left behind after an update or delete. PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control so writers create new versions and mark older versions invisible rather than rewriting pages in place. These invisible versions remain on disk until a cleanup step reclaims them. Over time, if many updates or deletes occur, the table and its indexes can grow much larger than the active data set, a condition we call table bloat. Bloat increases input and output for scans and index maintenance, can cause backups to take longer, and may trigger disk space alerts. A common misconception is that VACUUM always returns space to the operating system. Basic VACUUM marks space reusable within PostgreSQL but does not always shrink the file at the OS level; VACUUM FULL reclaims OS space but requires an exclusive lock. A concrete example: a log table that inserts and deletes many rows hourly will accumulate dead tuples quickly; running VACUUM or allowing autovacuum to respond reduces the internal bloat and keeps reads efficient. What metrics would you watch to detect bloat on a mission-critical table?

keyIdea.text: Dead tuples are obsolete row versions that consume space and slow scans. Detect and address bloat before it affects backups and queries.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Dead Tuples & Bloat
What is a dead tuple?

A dead tuple is a previously valid row version no longer visible to any transaction. It remains in the data file until reclaimed.

  • Accumulation causes table and index bloat.
  • Increased physical size leads to higher I/O and slower scans.
  • Reclaiming space can be internal or returned to the OS depending on the command.
Common misconception
Basic VACUUM reclaims space for reuse inside the database but does not always shrink the file seen by the operating system. VACUUM FULL does, but it locks the table.
Example scenario
A log_events table receives 100,000 inserts then half are deleted. pg_relation_size reports a large file despite fewer rows. This is classic bloat that VACUUM addresses.
Check: SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('log_events'));
Key Takeaway

Watch table size and scan times. Bloat is a performance and storage risk; reclaim proactively.

screens.title: VACUUM, VACUUM FULL, and autovacuum
screens.narratorSegment: VACUUM reclaims space occupied by dead tuples and marks it available for reuse inside PostgreSQL. It is safe to run routinely because it does not require exclusive table locks. VACUUM FULL is more aggressive: it rebuilds the table and returns disk space to the operating system, but it requires an exclusive lock and can block normal operations. This is why VACUUM FULL is reserved for maintenance windows or migration steps. PostgreSQL provides an autovacuum daemon that runs in the background to perform regular VACUUM and ANALYZE operations based on thresholds. Understanding autovacuum's behavior helps you decide whether manual intervention is needed after large bulk loads or deletes. A concrete example is running VACUUM ANALYZE on a table after a bulk import to update statistics and free internal space: the command combines space reclamation and statistics collection. Common mistakes include running VACUUM FULL on a busy production table or assuming autovacuum will keep up with an unusually high update rate. A safer alternative is scheduling manual VACUUM runs during off-peak times or adjusting autovacuum thresholds for heavy-write tables. After running maintenance, check pg_relation_size and query latency to confirm improvement. When would you choose VACUUM FULL despite its lock cost?

keyIdea.title: VACUUM modes
keyIdea.text: Use VACUUM regularly; reserve VACUUM FULL for maintenance windows. Autovacuum handles most workloads but tune it for heavy update patterns.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › VACUUM & Autovacuum
Command walkthrough
<!-- SQL examples for maintenance: --> -- Run VACUUM ANALYZE on a specific table VACUUM ANALYZE sales_data; -- Reclaim space to the OS (exclusive lock) VACUUM FULL sales_data; -- Show table size SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('sales_data'));
Safety note
VACUUM ANALYZE is non-blocking and ideal after many inserts. VACUUM FULL locks the table; schedule it during maintenance windows and ensure backups are recent.
Autovacuum behavior
Autovacuum runs automatically based on per-table thresholds. For workloads with many small updates, autovacuum should be tuned so it triggers frequently enough to prevent bloat. If autovacuum falls behind after a bulk load, run a manual VACUUM ANALYZE.
  • Autovacuum reduces manual effort but is not infallible.
  • Monitor autovacuum logs to see when it runs and what it does.
Check your work
After running maintenance, compare pg_relation_size before and after and note any change in query latency for representative queries.

screens.title: Reindexing, Integrity Checks, and Log Rotation
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes speed up lookups but they can fragment and bloat after many updates and deletes. Reindexing rebuilds an index to restore its efficiency and reclaim space. Use REINDEX TABLE or REINDEX INDEX when index bloat causes slow lookups or high maintenance overhead. Note that REINDEX can be resource intensive; PostgreSQL offers non-blocking alternatives such as creating an index concurrently. Data integrity checks verify that database files are not corrupted; these may be vendor-specific commands or extensions and should be part of periodic validation. Log files are another common source of disk growth. Continuous writes to database logs will fill disk if logs are not rotated and archived. Implement rotation and retention policies and archive old logs for later debugging. A practical example: if disk usage rises unexpectedly, first rotate and archive logs, then examine table sizes with pg_relation_size to find bloat. A common mistake is running a heavy reindex or vacuum full without checking log and backup state. Always ensure you have current backups before heavy maintenance. Which operation would you schedule first if you observe disk use suddenly climbing?

keyIdea.text: Reindex to restore index efficiency; run integrity checks to detect corruption; rotate logs to prevent disk exhaustion.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Reindexing & Logs
Reindexing options
Rebuilding an index can return space and improve lookup speed. Prefer non-blocking methods where available.
-- Reindex a specific table
REINDEX TABLE sales_data;

-- Reindex a specific index
REINDEX INDEX idx_sales_sale_date;

-- Non-blocking alternative when creating a new index
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_new ON sales_data (sale_date);
Note: REINDEX can be resource-intensive; schedule during low activity or use concurrent alternatives.
Integrity & logs
Run integrity checks appropriate to your database and rotate logs to avoid disk exhaustion. Old logs are useful for postmortem analysis but should be archived off the main disk.
Checklist: backup first • rotate logs • reindex if needed • monitor pg_relation_size
Concrete example
If disk fills quickly, rotate logs, archive old files, then check table and index sizes. If a single index is large and fragmented, plan a reindex during a maintenance window.
Common mistake
Running VACUUM FULL or REINDEX without recent backups and without considering lock impact can cause outages.

screens.title: A Systematic Troubleshooting Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When a database behaves unexpectedly, a clear workflow prevents wasted time. First, define the problem precisely: what errors appear, when did it start, and which users or queries are affected. Concrete examples help — is a single report failing or are all queries slow? Second, check basic connectivity and service health. A failed service or network block is often the simplest root cause. Third, inspect logs for explicit errors or repeated warnings; logs often contain the first clue. Fourth, monitor server resources — C P U spikes, memory pressure, or saturated disk input and output commonly manifest as slow queries. Fifth, inspect active queries to find long-running or blocked statements. Sixth, analyze slow queries with explain and timings to find missing indexes or poor plan choices. Finally, after isolating the root cause, apply a targeted fix and monitor to confirm recovery. A common misconception is to immediately change database configuration or restart services without collecting evidence; that can hide intermittent problems and cause downtime. Use this workflow to narrow causes quickly, run small non-destructive checks first, and escalate only when necessary. Try framing each incident as a short checklist: define, connect, logs, resources, active queries, analyze, fix. What single observation would you use to pick the right first diagnostic in your environment?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Systematic Troubleshooting Workflow
Checklist
  1. Define the problem: scope, users affected, and timeframe.
  2. Check connectivity: confirm service is running and ports are reachable.
  3. Examine logs: look for repeated errors, auth failures, or I/O warnings.
  4. Monitor resources: CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network use.
  5. Inspect active queries: identify blocked or long-running statements.
  6. Analyze and fix: use explain analyze, reindex, vacuum, or configuration tweaks as targeted remedies.
Example Scenario

A nightly ETL job slows select queries the next morning. Define: high I/O during peak reads. Connectivity: service reachable. Logs: frequent checkpoints and I/O warnings. Active queries: many waits for disk. Analysis shows table bloat and missing statistics. Targeted fixes: vacuum analyze and update stats, then re-evaluate query plans.

Key Takeaway

Follow a small, ordered checklist to avoid guesswork and reduce recovery time.

Workflow Diagram (conceptual)
A focused sequence to narrow root causes
1. Define
scope the issue
2. Connectivity
ping, service status
3. Logs
errors & warnings
4. Resources
CPU, I/O, memory
5. Active queries
pg_stat_activity
6. Analyze
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
Common Mistake

Restarting services before gathering logs or evidence can obscure intermittent problems and delay correct fixes.

Pro Tip

Record timestamps of failures so you can correlate log entries with resource spikes or scheduled jobs.

screens.title: Using Database Logs to Diagnose Problems
screens.narratorSegment: Database logs are the first place to look for clear, time-stamped evidence of what went wrong. Logs record authentication failures, configuration warnings, slow query reports, checkpoints, and disk input and output errors. A practical approach begins by narrowing a time window for the incident and searching for repeated messages, error codes, or stack traces. For example, seeing frequent 'could not write block' or 'out of memory' messages points quickly to disk or memory issues. If you see repeated authentication failures, focus on credentials, connection pools, or firewall changes. Rotated or archived logs matter: rotate logs regularly so the active file stays small and older logs are compressed for postmortem review. A common misconception is that raw logs are too noisy; instead, use simple filters — by timestamp, severity, and process id — to surface patterns. When investigating slow queries, correlate log entries that mark long durations with the corresponding S Q L text and execution plan. Always preserve relevant log files before restarting services. In short, logs give you context: they tell you what happened, when, and sometimes why. Practice searching logs with time filters and keep a short checklist of keywords to speed diagnosis. Which log message would you prioritize if you saw both an input and output warning and a repeated long-running query at the same time?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Database Logs
Log inspection example
Look for severity, timestamp, and repeated patterns
2026-09-01 02:03:12 UTC [12345] ERROR: could not write block 12345 to file "base/16384/67890": No space left on device
2026-09-01 02:03:12 UTC [12345] LOG: database system was interrupted; last known up at 2026-09-01 01:59:00 UTC
2026-09-01 02:04:01 UTC [12346] WARNING: duration: 12345.678 ms  execute : SELECT * FROM large_table WHERE user_id = 42;
2026-09-01 02:05:01 UTC [12347] FATAL: password authentication failed for user "data_user"
What to extract
  • Timestamp and PID to correlate with system metrics
  • Severity: ERROR or FATAL indicate urgent fixes
  • Repeated warnings show trends, not one-offs
Rotation & Archiving

Rotate logs to prevent disk exhaustion and compress older logs for investigations. Keep a short retention window that matches your SLA.

Quick Rule

Preserve logs that match the incident window before performing disruptive recoveries or restarts.

Log Filters

Use time ranges and severity filters to reduce noise. Grep or a log viewer can quickly surface repeating messages.

Example Search
# find errors in a time window
grep "2026-09-01 02:" postgresql.log | grep -i error
Scenario

If you see 'No space left on device' in logs, prioritize disk cleanup and avoid running heavy maintenance until space is reclaimed.

screens.title: Diagnosing Connectivity Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Connectivity errors are a frequent and approachable class of problems. When a client sees 'connection refused', it means the network path reached the host but the database port did not accept the connection. Start with the simplest checks: can you ping the host to confirm basic network reachability? Next, test the service port with a tool like telnet to confirm the process is listening on the expected port. If both fail, verify firewall rules and host-level service status. If network checks pass but the client still receives authentication failures, re-check credentials, connection string parameters, and whether the user account is allowed from that host. A common concrete example is a Python script using a database driver that fails because the port number in the configuration is incorrect; swapping to the correct port often resolves it immediately. Another common cause is a PostgreSQL instance that is running but bound only to localhost; remote clients will be refused until listen_addresses is adjusted. When debugging, collect these artifacts: ping/telnet outputs, service status, and a brief log excerpt at the same timestamp. A misconception is assuming connection refused is always an application bug; in practice, network or service configuration is more often at fault. Always confirm service health and port reachability before changing application code. After you fix connectivity, re-run the failing operation to confirm success. Which check would you run first in your environment and why?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Connectivity Diagnostics
Terminal checks

Use these commands to verify basic connectivity and listening ports

# check host reachability
ping -c 3 database_host

# check port (example for PostgreSQL default 5432)
telnet database_host 5432

# verify process on host (server-side)

Python connection example (visual)
import psycopg2
try:
  conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=prod user=data_user host=db.example.com port=5432 password=secret")
except psycopg2.OperationalError as e:
  print(f"Connection error: {e}")
Misconception

Assuming an application bug is the problem wastes time. Verify network and service first; often the fix is configuration or a firewall rule.

Checklist
  • Ping host; confirm packet reachability.
  • Telnet or equivalent to test TCP port.
  • Confirm service is running and listening on expected address.
  • Verify credentials and client IP authorization.
  • Check firewall rules and network ACLs.

If the server is listening only on localhost, set listen_addresses and restart the service during a maintenance window.

screens.title: Inspecting Active Queries and Resource Bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: Active queries and server resource metrics are where performance problems reveal themselves. The system view pg_stat_activity in PostgreSQL shows currently running queries, their state, start time, and waiting status. Use that view to locate queries that have been running unusually long or are in a waiting state because of locks or input and output. For MySQL, SHOW PROCESSLIST provides similar insight. While you monitor activity, also track C P U, memory, and disk input and output. High disk input and output with many sequential reads often points to table bloat or missing indexes; high C P U with low input and output may indicate expensive C P U-bound operations or complex joins. When you find a suspect query, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE to get an execution plan with real timing; that tells you whether the planner chose an index scan, sequential scan, or an expensive nested loop. A concrete example: a reporting query that scanned a large table due to a missing index, consuming disk input and output and blocking other queries. Adding an index or rewriting the query reduced input and output and unblocked the system. A common misconception is to kill queries as the first step; sometimes killing a heavy query is necessary, but it’s better to identify why the query was heavy and fix the root cause so it doesn't recur. After applying a fix, continue observing pg_stat_activity and resource metrics to confirm the improvement. Which metric change would convince you the issue is resolved?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Active Queries & Bottlenecks
Inspecting activity
Use system views to locate long-running or waiting queries
-- PostgreSQL: see active queries
SELECT pid, usename, state, query, now() - query_start AS duration
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY duration DESC LIMIT 10;
Analyze a slow query
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM large_table WHERE user_id = 42;
Takeaway

Combine activity views and resource metrics; plan fixes from EXPLAIN ANALYZE before rebuilding indexes or changing queries.

Resource indicators
  • High disk I/O → look for table bloat or sequential scans.
  • High CPU with low I/O → check complex computations or missing vectorized operations.
  • Many waiting states → investigate locks or contention.
When to kill a query

Only kill queries when they cause immediate system harm and you have a rollback plan; prefer to capture their plan and explain it first.

Concrete fix

If EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a sequential scan on a filtered column, consider adding an index or rewriting the query to use available indexes.

screens.title: Safe Maintenance Scheduling and Recovery Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Major maintenance actions such as VACUUM FULL, REINDEX, or restoring from backups can require exclusive locks or heavy resources. The safest strategy is to schedule these during off-peak windows and to communicate the maintenance window to stakeholders. Before any destructive or blocking operation, take a fresh backup so you can recover if something goes wrong. Consider non-blocking alternatives when available: in PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids exclusive locks when building an index, and autovacuum usually reduces the need for manual VACUUM FULL. When disk space is critically low, clean up large logs or temporary files, and prefer VACUUM (not VACUUM FULL) initially because VACUUM reclaims space internally without exclusive locks. If you must run VACUUM FULL or REINDEX, notify users, acquire a maintenance lock, and monitor the operation closely. Keep a rollback plan: know how to restore from the backup, and practice the restore procedure periodically so it completes within an acceptable time. A common mistake is performing heavy maintenance without checking replication lag or read-only replicas; ensure replicas are ready or taken out of rotation as needed. After maintenance, validate service health with a small set of smoke tests and check key query performance to confirm that the operation had the intended effect. In short: back up, prefer non-blocking options, schedule windows, notify stakeholders, and validate results. Which non-blocking alternative would you pick first in your environment?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Maintenance Scheduling
Maintenance timeline (example)
Plan, backup, run non-blocking options, escalate to blocking ops only if required
Plan & Notify
T-72h
Backup & Verify
T-24h
Non-blocking ops
T-2h
Blocking ops (if needed)
Window
Commands (visual)
-- Non-blocking index build
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_col ON table(col);

-- VACUUM ANALYZE example

Free quick space by removing old rotated logs or temporary files before running heavy operations. Avoid running VACUUM FULL until you have a backup and an outage window.

screens.title: Key Concepts

First, follow a repeatable troubleshooting workflow: define the problem, confirm connectivity, inspect logs, monitor resources, examine active queries, analyze slow statements, and then apply targeted fixes. Second, logs are essential evidence — use time and severity filters and preserve relevant files before disruptive actions. Third, connectivity issues often stem from network, service, or configuration problems rather than application bugs; use ping and port checks first. These small artifacts speed diagnosis and support safer maintenance decisions. Which of these concepts would change how you triage your next database incident?

fullNarratorScript:
Maintenance keeps a database healthy and predictable. Over time, updates and deletions leave behind overhead that slows queries and consumes disk space. In PostgreSQL this shows up as dead tuples and table bloat; routine commands reclaim space and refresh the planner's statistics so queries run efficiently. In this lesson you will learn what VACUUM and ANALYZE do, when to prefer lightweight background maintenance versus aggressive operations, and why some maintenance commands must be scheduled carefully to avoid locking production tables. We'll also preview reindexing, integrity checks, and log management so you can spot when a table or index needs attention. Finally, you'll be introduced to a practical activity that walks through creating simulated bloat, running VACUUM ANALYZE, and checking sizes before and after. By the end you will understand not just the commands but the operational trade-offs: which actions are safe to run continuously, which require a maintenance window, and how to measure success. Consider how routine care prevents surprises during critical analysis jobs or nightly batch runs. What maintenance step would you prioritize first on a heavily updated table?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify routine maintenance tasks a database needs, and explain why each one matters to performance and reliability. You will learn to describe how PostgreSQL handles row updates and why dead tuples accumulate, so you can diagnose table bloat. You will also practice running the core commands that reclaim space and refresh planner statistics. Finally, you will be guided through safety considerations for maintenance operations, including when to avoid blocking commands in production. Each objective emphasizes practical skill: reading sizes with pg_relation_size, choosing VACUUM versus VACUUM FULL, and recognizing when autovacuum has missed a workload spike. These are not abstract rules; they help you keep analysis jobs stable and reduce surprise outages during batch jobs. As you work through the lesson examples, you will gain a checklist for routine maintenance and a mental model for the trade-offs between lightweight background work and heavy, disruptive operations.

This set of objectives equips you with practical troubleshooting skills. You will learn a systematic approach to diagnose problems: define the issue precisely, check connectivity, inspect logs, and measure resource usage. You will practice using tools such as ping, telnet, pg_stat_activity, and pg_relation_size to collect evidence. You will also learn to analyze slow queries using execution plans and the role of ANALYZE in improving those plans. Finally, the objectives include handling common operational problems such as connection errors and disk space warnings, with concrete steps to resolve each. These skills help you understand whether a problem is a configuration or resource issue, a query design issue, or a maintenance backlog. Being methodical shortens downtime, reduces guesswork, and lets you escalate with clear evidence when you need help from a DBA. Practice each step until it becomes a clear checklist.

Databases need routine care because internal file structures evolve as data changes. When rows are updated or deleted, many systems do not immediately overwrite physical storage; instead they mark earlier versions as obsolete. Over time those obsolete entries accumulate, increasing the amount of data the server must scan for queries and the space required on disk. This leads to slower scans, higher input and output, and sometimes unexpected disk-full conditions during peak workloads. Maintenance tasks like VACUUM and reindexing remove or rebuild these remnants so the system can work with a leaner physical dataset. Beyond space, maintenance also keeps metadata and statistics accurate; stale statistics lead the planner to choose slower execution plans and make even well-indexed queries perform poorly. Neglect can also raise the chance of corruption going unnoticed, which is why integrity checks are part of routine work. A practical misconception is thinking that infrequent heavy maintenance is equivalent to continuous light maintenance. In practice, small automated actions are safer and keep disruption low. Which recurring checks would you include in a weekly maintenance checklist for a workload that writes a lot of small updates?

A dead tuple is an old row version left behind after an update or delete. PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control so writers create new versions and mark older versions invisible rather than rewriting pages in place. These invisible versions remain on disk until a cleanup step reclaims them. Over time, if many updates or deletes occur, the table and its indexes can grow much larger than the active data set, a condition we call table bloat. Bloat increases input and output for scans and index maintenance, can cause backups to take longer, and may trigger disk space alerts. A common misconception is that VACUUM always returns space to the operating system. Basic VACUUM marks space reusable within PostgreSQL but does not always shrink the file at the OS level; VACUUM FULL reclaims OS space but requires an exclusive lock. A concrete example: a log table that inserts and deletes many rows hourly will accumulate dead tuples quickly; running VACUUM or allowing autovacuum to respond reduces the internal bloat and keeps reads efficient. What metrics would you watch to detect bloat on a mission-critical table?

VACUUM reclaims space occupied by dead tuples and marks it available for reuse inside PostgreSQL. It is safe to run routinely because it does not require exclusive table locks. VACUUM FULL is more aggressive: it rebuilds the table and returns disk space to the operating system, but it requires an exclusive lock and can block normal operations. This is why VACUUM FULL is reserved for maintenance windows or migration steps. PostgreSQL provides an autovacuum daemon that runs in the background to perform regular VACUUM and ANALYZE operations based on thresholds. Understanding autovacuum's behavior helps you decide whether manual intervention is needed after large bulk loads or deletes. A concrete example is running VACUUM ANALYZE on a table after a bulk import to update statistics and free internal space: the command combines space reclamation and statistics collection. Common mistakes include running VACUUM FULL on a busy production table or assuming autovacuum will keep up with an unusually high update rate. A safer alternative is scheduling manual VACUUM runs during off-peak times or adjusting autovacuum thresholds for heavy-write tables. After running maintenance, check pg_relation_size and query latency to confirm improvement. When would you choose VACUUM FULL despite its lock cost?

Indexes speed up lookups but they can fragment and bloat after many updates and deletes. Reindexing rebuilds an index to restore its efficiency and reclaim space. Use REINDEX TABLE or REINDEX INDEX when index bloat causes slow lookups or high maintenance overhead. Note that REINDEX can be resource intensive; PostgreSQL offers non-blocking alternatives such as creating an index concurrently. Data integrity checks verify that database files are not corrupted; these may be vendor-specific commands or extensions and should be part of periodic validation. Implement rotation and retention policies and archive old logs for later debugging. A practical example: if disk usage rises unexpectedly, first rotate and archive logs, then examine table sizes with pg_relation_size to find bloat. A common mistake is running a heavy reindex or vacuum full without checking log and backup state. Always ensure you have current backups before heavy maintenance. Third, inspect logs for explicit errors or repeated warnings; logs often contain the first clue.
